analysis.one_liner: Exempts forestry runoff from Clean Water Act discharge permits.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have freed timber operations from federal water pollution permits, was referred to committee and never came to a vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Water Act so that stormwater running off forestry work — site preparation, replanting, thinning, prescribed burns, pest control, harvesting, drainage, road building, and tree nurseries — could not be covered by federal water pollution permits. It would also have barred the EPA from requiring states, even indirectly, to permit those discharges. The bill never left the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Timber companies and forest landowners would avoid the cost and paperwork of federal Clean Water Act permits for runoff from logging, road building, and related forestry work. The bill would also lock that exemption in by removing these discharges from the law's definition of a 'point source,' the term the Clean Water Act uses to cover discharges that require permits [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Would prohibit the EPA from requiring a national pollutant discharge elimination system (NPDES) permit — the Clean Water Act's main discharge permit — for stormwater runoff from nine categories of silvicultural activity, including harvesting, road construction and maintenance, and nursery operations [S2][S3].
Would bar the EPA from 'directly or indirectly' requiring any state to require such permits, and would rewrite the definition of 'point source' so these forestry discharges fall outside it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Downstream communities would bear the cost: sediment and other pollutants washing off logging roads and harvest sites would no longer be subject to federal permit requirements or state permitting that EPA could compel, leaving water quality protections to whatever voluntary or state-level rules existed without a federal backstop [S3].

drawbacks.text: The exemption would cover road construction and maintenance in forests, a well-known source of sediment in streams, with no federal permit or monitoring requirement to catch problems [S3].

By removing these discharges from the 'point source' definition, the bill would weaken not just permit requirements but the Clean Water Act framework built around them, and would prevent EPA from pushing states to fill the gap [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Forestry operators had a real argument that NPDES permitting for routine logging and road work is costly and poorly suited to diffuse, weather-driven runoff, and many states already use forestry best-management practices. But this bill went further than accommodating that concern: it would have permanently removed these discharges from the federal permitting system and barred EPA from pressing states to cover them, shifting the water quality cost onto people downstream. The bill never advanced, so neither the relief nor the cost happened.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which held a related hearing in the Agriculture Committee but never reported the bill, and it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Blanche Lincoln (D-AR) introduced the bill on February 8, 2000, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S5].
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
On February 23, 2000, the Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee held a hearing on the measure, printed as S.Hrg. 106-699 [S5].
The Environment and Public Works Committee never reported the bill and the full Senate never voted on it; the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Downstream communities and anyone who fishes, swims, or drinks from forest streams are better off, since forestry runoff remains subject to the Clean Water Act's permitting framework. Timber operators did not get the exemption they sought.

for.name: Sen. Blanche Lincoln
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out for a Senate vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its only cosponsor were both Democrats, and no floor vote ever occurred, so there is no record of how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have exempted logging, forest road building, and related work from federal water pollution permits, saving operators compliance costs while leaving runoff from those activities outside the permitting system. The industry's gain would come at the expense of downstream water quality.

industries.industry: EPA and state water permitting agencies
industries.note: The bill would have stripped EPA of authority to require NPDES permits for forestry runoff and barred it from pushing states to require them, narrowing the agencies' water quality toolkit.
